questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
Will they release the new season next month?

options.text: Will the new season be released next month?
Will the new season be release by them next month?
Will the new season be releasing next month?
Will the new season released by them next month?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Will the new season be released next month?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence is an **interrogative sentence** in the **Simple Future Tense** (Active Voice).
 
• In the **Active Voice**, the structure for a **Simple Future** question is: **Will + Subject + V1 (Base Form) + Object?**
 
• To convert this into the **Passive Voice**, the grammatical formula changes to: **Will + Object (acting as Subject) + be + V3 (Past Participle) + (by + Agent)?**
 
• In this conversion, the object **the new season** shifts to the subject position, and the verb **release** is transformed into its third form, **released**.
 
• The auxiliary verb **be** must be placed before the **past participle** to complete the passive construction in the future tense.
 
• In English grammar, the agent (e.g., **by them**) is often omitted in the **Passive Voice** if the subject is a general or indefinite pronoun like **they**, **people**, or **someone**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Simple Future Passive Rules**:
 
 
• **Affirmative Structure**: Subject + **will be** + **V3** (e.g., The season will be released).
 
• **Negative Structure**: Subject + **will not be** + **V3** (e.g., The season will not be released).
 
• **Interrogative Structure**: **Will** + Subject + **be** + **V3**? (e.g., Will the season be released?).
 
 
 
• **Structural Analysis of Incorrect Options**:
 
 
• The use of the base form **release** instead of the **past participle** is a common error in passive constructions, as seen in the second option.
 
• The **Future Continuous** form (e.g., **be releasing**) denotes an ongoing action in the future and does not satisfy the requirements of a standard passive conversion for the simple future.
 
• The omission of the verb **be** in an interrogative passive sentence renders the sentence grammatically incomplete and incorrect.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
By the end of the year, I will have completed my internship.

options.text: By the end of the year, my internship will have completed.
By the end of the year, my internship will have been completed.
By the end of the year, my internship has been completed.
By the end of the year, my internship will be completed.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By the end of the year, my internship will have been completed.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence **By the end of the year, I will have completed my internship** is in the **Active Voice** and uses the **Future Perfect Tense**.

• The **Active Voice** structure for **Future Perfect** is: **Subject (I) + will have + Past Participle (completed) + Object (my internship)**.

• To convert this into **Passive Voice**, the **Object** of the active sentence (**my internship**) becomes the **Subject** of the passive sentence.

• The structural formula for **Future Perfect** in the **Passive Voice** is: **New Subject + will have been + Past Participle (V3) + (by + agent)**.

• The auxiliary verb **been** is mandatory when converting any perfect tense (Present, Past, or Future) into its passive form to indicate the state of completion.

• Applying these rules, the verb **will have completed** is transformed into **will have been completed**.

• The adverbial phrase **By the end of the year** denotes the future time limit and remains at the beginning of the sentence to maintain the original emphasis on the deadline.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Grammatical Tense Analysis**:

• **Future Perfect Tense**: Used to describe an action that will be **finished** by a particular time in the future. In passive voice, the focus remains on the **completion** of the task (the internship) rather than the person doing it.

• **Incorrect Options**:

• **will have completed**: This is active voice; it implies the internship itself is performing the action.

• **has been completed**: This is **Present Perfect Passive**, which refers to an action completed in the past or very recently, not in the future.

• **will be completed**: This is **Simple Future Passive**, which does not convey the sense of an action being finished **by** a specific point in time.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
The castle had been visited by thousands of tourists before the storm.

options.text: Thousands of tourists visited the castle before the storm.
Thousands of tourists were visiting the castle before the storm.
Thousands of tourists had visited the castle before the storm.
Thousands of tourists will visit the castle before the storm.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Thousands of tourists had visited the castle before the storm.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence is in the **Passive Voice** and uses the **Past Perfect Tense**, identified by the structure **had been + past participle** (visited).

• In **Passive Voice**, the object of the action (the castle) serves as the grammatical subject, while the actual doer (thousands of tourists) is introduced by the preposition **by**.

• To convert a sentence from **Passive Voice** to **Active Voice** in the **Past Perfect Tense**, the structure must follow the formula: **Subject + had + past participle (V3) + object**.

• The doer of the action, **thousands of tourists**, is moved to the subject position at the beginning of the sentence.

• The auxiliary verb **been** is removed, and the auxiliary **had** is paired directly with the **past participle** verb **visited** to maintain the **Active Voice** form.

• The original subject, **the castle**, becomes the **direct object** of the verb in the active construction.

• The temporal phrase **before the storm** remains at the end of the sentence to indicate the sequence of events.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Voice and Tense Consistency**:

• **Simple Past Tense**: Converts to **Subject + V2 + Object** (e.g., Thousands of tourists visited...). This does not match the **Past Perfect** aspect of the original sentence.

• **Past Continuous Tense**: Uses the structure **was/were + verb + ing** (e.g., were visiting). This implies an ongoing action, which contradicts the completed nature of **Past Perfect**.

• **Future Simple Tense**: Uses **will + base verb** (e.g., will visit). This changes the timeframe from the past to the future, making it grammatically incorrect in this context.

• The **Past Perfect Tense** is specifically used to describe an action that was completed before another point or action in the past (the storm).

</ul

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

Reeta was very much depressed ______ her separation from her family.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**about**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The preposition '**about**' is used to indicate the **subject**, **cause**, or **reason** for a particular feeling or emotional state. 
• In this context, the sentence explains the reason behind **Reeta's** emotional state of being '**depressed**.' The reason is her '**separation from her family**.' 
• The construction '**depressed about**' is the idiomatic way to express sadness or low spirits regarding a specific situation or event. 
• **Options 1, 2,** and **4** are grammatically or idiomatically unsuitable for indicating the cause of depression in this specific sentence structure. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**. **Complete Sentence:** *'Reeta was very much **depressed about**__ her separation from her family.'* **__Additional Information__** 
• **Option 1: 'for'** is generally used to indicate purpose, duration, or a recipient (e.g., 'waiting for someone'), which does not fit here. 
• **Option 2: 'at'** is often used for reactions to a specific point or event (e.g., 'surprised at'), but 'about' is preferred for situational causes of depression. 
• **Option 4: 'in'** is used to indicate a state (e.g., 'in a depression') or a physical location, but not the external cause of the feeling. </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."

The politician's sudden change of stance was clearly __an attempt to fish into troubled waters.__

options.text: an attempt for fishing out troubled waters
the attempt to fish under troubled waters
an attempt to fish in troubled waters

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**an attempt to fish in troubled waters**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence requires the correct use of a standard **English idiom**. The expression **to fish in troubled waters** is a fixed phrase used to describe the act of taking advantage of a **disturbed**, **chaotic**, or **unstable situation** for personal gain.
 
• In the original sentence, the preposition **into** was used incorrectly. Idioms are **lexically fixed**, meaning their components, including **prepositions**, cannot be changed without making the phrase grammatically or idiomatically incorrect.
 
• The use of the preposition **in** is essential because it signifies being within the state of **turmoil** or **trouble**. The politician in the sentence is attempting to benefit from the existing confusion, which is perfectly captured by the phrase **an attempt to fish in troubled waters**.
 
• Options 1 and 2 are incorrect because they use improper prepositions such as **for**, **out**, and **under**, which do not exist in the standard version of this **metaphorical expression**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Etymology and Origin:**
 
 
• The idiom dates back to the **16th century** and is derived from the literal practice of fishing. It was observed that fish are more easily caught when the water is **agitated** or **murky**, as they become disoriented and cannot see the **nets** or **hooks** clearly.
 
• The first recorded use in **English literature** appeared in **1568** in a collection of prose, where it was used to describe people who benefit from **civil discord**.
 
 
 
• **Grammatical Function:**
 
 
• **Prepositional usage:** In English, **in** often denotes a state or condition (e.g., in trouble, in love), whereas **into** denotes movement or transformation. Since the 'waters' (trouble) already exist, the **locative preposition** 'in' is the only correct choice.
 
• **Noun Phrase Structure:** The phrase **an attempt to** is followed by an **infinitive verb** (to fish), forming a cohesive **adjectival phrase** that modifies the politician's action.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."

Whether we take the early flight or the late one __is a mute point__ since we're already behind schedule.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**is a moot point**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase **moot point** is an **idiomatic expression** referring to a subject that has **no practical significance** or is **irrelevant** because the situation has already been decided by other factors.
 
• In the provided sentence, the choice between an **early flight** or a **late flight** is considered **insignificant** because the travelers are **already behind schedule**, making the timing of the flight **purely academic** or **pointless**.
 
• The term **moot** originates from **Old English** 'mot', meaning a **meeting** or **assembly** for debate. In **legal terminology**, a **moot court** is a mock trial for students to practice **hypothetical cases** that have no **binding authority** or real-world effect.
 
• Using **mute** instead of **moot** is a common **linguistic error** known as an **eggcorn**. While **mute** means silent, it does not convey the intended meaning of **irrelevance** in a debate or decision-making context.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Common Confusions**:
 
 
• **Muted point**: The word **muted** refers to something that is **softened**, **subdued**, or **quieted** (e.g., **muted colors** or **muted sounds**). It is **grammatically incorrect** in this idiomatic context.
 
• **Mute**: This word describes a **lack of speech** or **silence**. It is often used in **technology** (the **mute button**) or **media** to indicate the **absence of audio**.
 
• **Moot** as a verb: Beyond being an adjective, **moot** can function as a **verb** meaning to **propose** or **bring up** a topic for **discussion**. For example, 'The proposal for a new park was **mooted** during the city council meeting.'
 
 
</ul
